data.title: Androgenetic alopecia — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 29 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Androgenetic alopecia** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define androgenetic alopecia (AGA).**
- Common, genetically determined, androgen-dependent, progressive non-scarring hair loss characterised by follicular miniaturisation in a patterned distribution; male pattern hair loss (MPHL) and female pattern hair loss (FPHL)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Genetic susceptibility (polygenic — androgen receptor gene on X chromosome, chromosome 20p11) + androgens: testosterone converted by 5α-reductase type 2 (outer root sheath/dermal papilla) to DHT → binds androgen receptors in dermal papilla of susceptible follicles → shortening of anagen and progressive miniaturisation (terminal → vellus-like), increased telogen; perifollicular micro-inflammation and fibrosis
- Occipital follicles are androgen-insensitive — basis for hair transplantation (donor dominance)
- FPHL: less clearly androgen-dependent; hyperandrogenism in some (PCOS)

**Q3. Discuss classifications (PYQ: AGA with a note on…).**
- Men: Hamilton–Norwood (I–VII; frontotemporal recession and vertex thinning; type A variant), BASP classification
- Women: Ludwig (I–III diffuse thinning of crown with preserved frontal hairline), Olsen ('Christmas tree' pattern — frontal accentuation), Sinclair (1–5) visual scale; Savin scale

**Q4. Clinical features.**
- MPHL: onset after puberty; bitemporal recession and vertex thinning progressing to bald crown with retained occipital/parietal fringe
- FPHL: diffuse thinning over crown and widening of central parting with intact frontal hairline; may begin at puberty or menopause
- Signs of hyperandrogenism in women: hirsutism, acne, irregular menses, AN (SAHA syndrome — Seborrhoea, Acne, Hirsutism, Alopecia)

**Q5. Trichoscopy.**
- Hair shaft diameter diversity >20% (key sign), increased vellus hairs, perifollicular brown halo (peripilar sign), yellow dots (few), single-hair follicular units, frontal > occipital difference (useful in FPHL)

**Q6. Discuss evaluation of hair loss (PYQ).**
- History: onset, duration, pattern, shedding vs thinning, family history, diet, drugs, illness/surgery 2–3 months before, menstrual/obstetric history, hair care practices
- Examination: pattern, scalp (scarring, scaling, erythema), hair pull test (>6 hairs/10% = active shedding), hair density, trichoscopy, signs of hyperandrogenism, nails, body hair
- Investigations: CBC, ferritin (aim >40–70 ng/ml), TSH, vitamin D, B12, zinc; women with hyperandrogenism — total/free testosterone, DHEAS, prolactin, 17-OH progesterone, pelvic USG; trichogram, biopsy (horizontal sections — terminal:vellus ratio <4:1 in AGA vs 7:1 normal) when doubtful

**Q7. Discuss drugs used in AGA including anti-androgens (PYQ).**
- Topical minoxidil 5% (men), 2–5% (women) twice daily or foam — prolongs anagen, increases follicle size (potassium channel opener, vasodilator); initial shedding at 2–8 weeks; results at 4–6 months; must continue
- Oral finasteride 1 mg/day (men) — 5α-reductase type 2 inhibitor, reduces scalp DHT ~60%; side effects — sexual dysfunction (low libido, erectile dysfunction ~1–2%), gynaecomastia, depression (post-finasteride syndrome debated), lowers PSA by ~50%; teratogenic to male fetus (women of child-bearing age must not take/handle broken tablets)
- Dutasteride 0.5 mg (types 1 and 2 inhibitor; more potent) — oral or mesotherapy
- Topical finasteride 0.25% spray (lower systemic exposure)
- Low-dose oral minoxidil 0.25–5 mg/day (men and women) — side effects hypertrichosis, pedal oedema, tachycardia, postural hypotension
- Women: spironolactone 50–200 mg/day, cyproterone acetate (with ethinyl oestradiol), flutamide/bicalutamide (hepatotoxicity monitoring), OCP with anti-androgenic progestins; finasteride/dutasteride only in post-menopausal women
- Adjuncts: PRP injections, microneedling (with minoxidil), low-level laser therapy (LLLT), ketoconazole 2% shampoo, nutritional correction (iron, vitamin D)
- Hair transplantation: follicular unit transplantation (strip/FUT) or follicular unit extraction (FUE) — for stable disease, adequate donor area; continue medical therapy
- Camouflage: scalp micropigmentation, fibres, wigs

**Q8. Discuss the effects of drugs on hair (PYQ).**
- Drug-induced hair loss: anagen effluvium (chemotherapy — cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, taxanes; within 1–4 weeks), telogen effluvium (retinoids, anticoagulants — heparin, warfarin; β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, antithyroids, anticonvulsants — valproate, lithium, OCP withdrawal, interferons, statins)
- Drug-induced hypertrichosis/hirsutism: minoxidil, cyclosporine, phenytoin, diazoxide, streptomycin, steroids, danazol, testosterone, latanoprost (eyelashes), EGFR inhibitors (trichomegaly)
- Hair colour change: chloroquine (bleaching), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib — depigmentation; or darkening), PD-1 inhibitors; curling with retinoids/EGFR inhibitors

**Q9. Prognosis.**
- Progressive without treatment; early treatment preserves rather than fully restores; effect lost within months of stopping

**Q10. Describe the Hamilton–Norwood classification.**
- Male pattern: I — minimal frontotemporal recession; II — symmetrical triangular frontotemporal recession; III — deep recession (III vertex — vertex thinning with stage II recession); IV — further recession + vertex balding separated by band; V — band narrower; VI — bridge lost, confluent; VII — only horseshoe band at sides and back; type A variants — anterior-to-posterior progression without vertex

**Q11. Describe the Ludwig and Sinclair scales for female pattern hair loss.**
- Ludwig: grade I — mild crown thinning with preserved frontal hairline; II — marked; III — near-total crown baldness
- Sinclair: 1–5 based on widening of the central part (stage 1 normal → 5 advanced); Olsen 'Christmas tree' pattern — frontal accentuation of part widening

**Q12. Explain the pathogenesis in detail.**
- Genetic (polygenic — androgen receptor gene on X chromosome, EDA2R, 20p11) + androgens: testosterone converted to DHT by 5α-reductase type 2 (and 1) in dermal papilla → DHT binds AR → shortening of anagen, progressive follicular miniaturisation (terminal → vellus-like), increased telogen
- Other factors: perifollicular micro-inflammation and fibrosis, Wnt/β-catenin down-regulation, PGD2 (inhibits hair growth) increase, ageing, oxidative stress

**Q13. Trichoscopy features.**
- Hair shaft thickness variability >20% (anisotrichosis), increased vellus hairs, yellow dots (few), perifollicular brown halo (peripilar sign), single-hair follicular units, scalp pigmentation honeycomb; frontal more than occipital differences

**Q14. Minoxidil — mechanism, use and side effects.**
- Potassium-channel opener → vasodilation, prolongs anagen, enlarges miniaturised follicles, VEGF up-regulation; topical 5% (men; 2–5% women) twice daily or foam; effect after 3–6 months, maintained only while used
- Low-dose oral minoxidil 0.25–5 mg/day — increasingly used (better adherence); side effects — hypertrichosis, pedal oedema, tachycardia, postural hypotension; topical — irritant/allergic dermatitis (propylene glycol), initial shedding, facial hypertrichosis
- Sulfotransferase activity in follicle predicts response

**Q15. Finasteride and dutasteride.**
- Finasteride 1 mg/day (type 2 5α-reductase inhibitor — reduces scalp DHT ~60%); dutasteride 0.5 mg (types 1 and 2, more potent); effect after 6–12 months; side effects — reduced libido, erectile dysfunction (~1–2%), gynaecomastia, depression ('post-finasteride syndrome' debated); lowers PSA by ~50% (double the value for screening); teratogenic — women of child-bearing potential shouldn't handle crushed tablets
- Topical finasteride 0.25% spray — lower systemic levels

**Q16. Treatment of female pattern hair loss.**
- Topical minoxidil 2–5%, low-dose oral minoxidil, anti-androgens (spironolactone 50–200 mg/day, cyproterone acetate with OCP, flutamide/ bicalutamide), finasteride/ dutasteride in post-menopausal women (contraception if pre-menopausal), correct iron/ thyroid, PRP, LLLT, camouflage, hair transplant

**Q17. Platelet-rich plasma and other procedures.**
- PRP: autologous platelet concentrate (growth factors — PDGF, VEGF, EGF) injected into scalp monthly × 3 then every 3–6 months; modest evidence
- Microneedling (with minoxidil), low-level laser therapy (650–900 nm) devices, botulinum toxin (limited), mesotherapy; hair transplant — follicular unit transplantation (strip) or follicular unit extraction (FUE); need stable donor area and medical therapy to maintain native hair

**Q18. Evaluation of a woman with hair loss — what history and tests?**
- Duration, pattern (diffuse vs patterned), shedding vs thinning, menstrual history, hirsutism/ acne, pregnancy, diet/ weight loss, drugs, illness, family history; examine part width, hair pull, trichoscopy
- Tests: CBC, ferritin (aim >40–70 ng/ml), TSH, vitamin D, B12, zinc; androgen profile if signs of hyperandrogenism; scalp biopsy (horizontal sections) when diagnosis unclear

**Q19. Histopathology of AGA on horizontal sections.**
- Increased vellus-like (miniaturised) hairs with terminal:vellus ratio <4:1 (normal ~7:1), increased telogen, fibrous streamers beneath miniaturised follicles, mild perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation, normal total follicle number (non-scarring)

**Q20. Drugs causing hair loss (PYQ: effects of drugs on hair).**
- Anagen effluvium: chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, taxanes), colchicine, thallium, radiation
- Telogen effluvium: anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin), antithyroid drugs, β-blockers, retinoids (acitretin, isotretinoin), lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, oral contraceptive withdrawal, ACE inhibitors, statins, interferon, antidepressants
- Hypertrichosis/hirsutism: minoxidil, cyclosporine, phenytoin, androgens, steroids, diazoxide, latanoprost (eyelashes), PUVA
- Hair colour changes: chloroquine (lightening), tyrosine kinase inhibitors, cyclosporine/ EGFR inhibitors (curly hair)

**Q21. What is frontal fibrosing alopecia and why differentiate?**
- Scarring alopecia (LPP variant) in post-menopausal women — band-like recession of frontal/ temporal hairline with perifollicular erythema/ scale, loss of eyebrows, lonely hairs, facial papules; association with sunscreen/ leave-on cosmetics debated
- Differs from AGA (non-scarring, preserved follicular openings); treat with 5-α-reductase inhibitors, HCQ, intralesional steroids, low-dose isotretinoin

**Q22. AGA and systemic associations.**
- Early-onset AGA in men associated with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, coronary heart disease, benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension; early 'male PCOS' phenotype; screen cardiovascular risk factors in young men with severe early AGA

**Q23. Counselling points in AGA treatment.**
- Medical therapy aims to stop progression and partial regrowth; initial shedding with minoxidil in first 2–8 weeks; assessment at 6 and 12 months with standardised photographs; must continue indefinitely; combination therapy better; realistic expectations and camouflage options (fibres, tinted sprays, wigs, scalp micropigmentation)

**Q24. Differential diagnosis of patterned hair loss.**
- Telogen effluvium, diffuse AA, frontal fibrosing alopecia, LPP, traction alopecia (frontotemporal in tight hairstyles), trichotillomania, hypothyroidism, iron deficiency, secondary syphilis, SLE

**Q25. What is the 'senescent alopecia'?**
- Age-related diffuse thinning after 60 years without miniaturisation pattern or androgen dependency — uniform reduction of follicles and diameter; may overlap with AGA

**Q26. What newer drugs are in development for AGA?**
- Topical clascoterone solution (androgen receptor antagonist), pyrilutamide, KX-826, JAK inhibitors (topical — studied), Wnt activators, botulinum toxin, exosomes and stem-cell-derived products (unproven) — check status before quoting

**Q27. What are the side effects of hair transplant?**
- Folliculitis, cysts, scalp numbness, shock loss of native hair, 'pluggy' appearance (older techniques), donor-site scarring (strip), unnatural hairline, infection, bleeding

**Q28. What scales measure hair growth in trials?**
- Global photographic assessment, phototrichogram/ trichoscan (hair count and density in a target area — 1 cm²), hair weight, patient self-assessment questionnaires

**Q29. Why does the occiput not bald in AGA?**
- Occipital follicles have fewer androgen receptors and less 5α-reductase activity — 'donor dominance' (transplanted occipital follicles maintain resistance at recipient site)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bitemporal recession + vertex thinning, hair diameter diversity >20% — AGA
- Finasteride 1 mg + minoxidil 5% — men; spironolactone/minoxidil — women

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Androgenetic alopecia); Hamilton–Norwood and Ludwig classifications. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
